note: A mode drilled by its one changed note: hear natural minor switch to Dorian on a two-scales play-along, find the 6th in the position with the root on the low E string, then in the position with the root on the A string over a drone. The key is moves (any key), so the title names it as {{=key}}, notes are degrees, and a {{?key}} line says what stays the same; positions are named by where the root sits. Folds in the D Dorian version of the same drill.

exercise.title: {{=key}} Dorian: find the 6th
exercise.why: Dorian and natural minor on the same root differ by one note, the 6th, so that note is the only place the mode can be heard: find it first, then aim for it.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the drone on {{1}} and the metronome for eight bars: four in {{=key}} natural minor, then four in {{=key}} Dorian. Play each scale from its lowest {{1}} up and back down along with the neck, and listen for the bar where one note changes.
The faded note is the one to leave out: {{6}} in the first half, {{b6}} in the second.

cells.heading: Root on the low E string

cells.text:
The note that changed is {{6}}: tap it on the neck below to hear it. The neck shows the {{=key}} Dorian scale in the position with {{1}} on the low E string. Start on the ringed {{1}} on the low E string, play up to the high e string and back down, then make up short phrases that pass through {{6}}.
Practice until your fingers reach for {{6}} without you looking for it.

Press Play below to start the drone on {{1}}. Under it is the same scale in the position with {{1}} on the A string: play it up and back down, and stop for a moment on each ringed {{6}}.
Listen for {{6}} against the drone: it is the note that makes the scale sound brighter than natural minor.
{{?key}}In another key both positions sit on other frets, and {{6}} keeps its place inside each one.
